title: the wire of Yeah speaks ACP, the queue events travel only where they were asked for, and the bytes on the wire are the bytes of the text
intent: The integration with Paseo exposed a defect of the wire that no offline check had caught, because every offline check was written by the same hand as the code and read the wire the way the code wrote it.  A client that validates the wire refused every `session/update' of Yeah: the content of a chunk was an array of content blocks where ACP says one block, and the events of the pending queue (`input_queued', `input_taken', `input_recovered', `input_withdrawn') travelled to every client although ACP has no such kinds.  The refusal was total — the text of the agent, the calls of its tools and the state of its queue never reached the client, and the client saw a run without a word.  Wave 40 repairs both shapes: the content of a chunk is one content block, as the schema of the wire says, and the events of the queue are an extension that travels only to the client that asked for them in the `_meta' of its capabilities at `initialize'.  The name of the extension, the version of the protocol and the way the announcement is read live in one file, `lib/yeah-acp-vocabulary.el', which both sides of Yeah require.  The second half of the wave answers the question the first half left open: the shapes of the wire were right, and the text of the agent still did not reach the client.  The model of the live task answered only with the call of the `finish' tool, the `finish' tool was not projected at all, and the client saw a `tool_call' without a word of the answer in it.  A client that speaks ACP expects the words of the agent as the message of the agent, so the summary of a finished run is projected as `agent_message_chunk', and the call of a tool carries what it was called with and what it returned (`rawInput' and `rawOutput').  The journal holds the arguments of a call in their printed form, so the printed form is read back into the values themselves — and, because the arguments come from the model, it is read as data and never as code.  The third part of the wave answers the question the second half left open: the text of the agent reached the client — the live check in Paseo showed the answer of the model in the timeline of the agent — and the words of it were mojibake.  The journal of the session held the right text, so the spoiling happened on the way out: `json-serialize' returns a unibyte string whose bytes are UTF-8, and `princ' of such a string makes Emacs read every byte as a character of Latin-1 and write the characters back as UTF-8.  Every non-ASCII answer was written twice over.  The wire now writes the bytes of a message as they are (`lib/yeah-wire.el'), and both protocols that write to a stream use it.
objection: The wave changes the wire of Yeah for every client, not only for the one that found the defect.  A client that read the content of a chunk as an array of blocks must read one block now, and a client that wanted the events of the queue without announcing them must announce them: the events of the queue are not ACP, and a client that refuses an update it does not know refuses the whole update.  The editor of Yeah announces them, so the editor keeps the queue it had.  The wave does not add the ACP methods that an orchestrator expects and that Yeah does not have — `session/set_mode', the change of the model of a session and the `mcpServers' of a session — and it does not make the tools of a run work in the directory of the session; those are gaps of the surface, and they are written down in docs/PLAN.md 17.1.  The claim of the wave is bound to a check that reads the kinds of the updates from the schema of the wire, so the schema and the code cannot drift apart without the check failing.
refuted_by: a session/update names a kind that the schema of the wire does not declare, or the content of a chunk is an array of blocks instead of one block; a client that announced nothing receives a queue event, or a client that announced them receives none; the client receives no message of the agent, or receives one without the words of the run; a tool call reaches the client as a name without its arguments, or without the result of the call; the bytes the server writes for a non-ASCII answer differ from the UTF-8 of that answer, or carry it written twice over
note: All four controls were run against the code of this wave and bit.  The control of `the-wire-speaks-acp' turns the content of a chunk back into an array, and the check fails on the assertion that the chunk carries one content block (`wire: the chunk did not carry one content block: ((:type "text" :text "wait"))').  The control of `the-queue-events-travel-where-they-were-asked-for' lets the queue events travel to every client, and the check fails on two assertions: the client that announced nothing received the update `input_queued', and the queue events reached a client that announced nothing.  The control of `the-answer-of-the-agent-reaches-the-client' renames the kind of the finished run, and the check fails on the assertion that the answer of the agent reached the client.  The control of `a-tool-call-carries-its-input-and-its-output' takes the input of the call away, and the unit check fails on the assertion that the call carries its arguments.  The wave also repairs the control of the claim `wire-stdio', whose constant had moved to the vocabulary of the wire: the control now names the file the constant lives in, and the scope of the claim names it too.  The claim `the-wire-carries-the-control' says now that the queue of the session reaches the client that asked for the queue events, and not every client.  The wave found three defects of its own code before the checks caught them: Emacs parses a JSON object into a property list whose keys are keywords, so the key of the announcement was a keyword and not the plain symbol the first version looked for; in a `pcase' pattern a symbol is a variable that binds the matched value and not a test, so the gate of the queue events did not hold — the compiler warned about the unused argument and the canary failed when the control was applied; and Emacs 30 does not read `#.\'' any more, so the reading of the printed form of the arguments does not need the variable `*read-eval\'', and the guard against a form that would be evaluated is a plain test of the printed form.  The fifth claim, `the-text-on-the-wire-is-the-text-the-model-wrote', was born from the live check: the answer of the model reached the timeline of the agent in Paseo and was mojibake (`Emacs Ð¼ ýÑ‚Ð¾ …'), while the journal of the session held the right text.  The bytes were spoiled on the way out, and no offline check had seen it, because every offline check read the wire through a character set instead of through the bytes.  The new check (`tests/checks/check-wire-carries-the-text.el') reads the bytes of a real server process and compares them with the UTF-8 of the answer; its control removes the decoding of the bytes and the check fails with `the text of the answer is not on the wire as it was written'.  The control was run against the code of this wave and bit.  The wave also found that the working directory of a session (`cwd') is still not applied to the tools: in the live check the `bash' of the agent ran in the directory of the process, not in the repository of the task — that gap is written down in docs/PLAN.md 17.1 and was not closed here.
